I’m 62 this year, and I’ve worked these fields long enough to know I can’t chase every new idea. I still mainly follow what has worked on my own land and what the better growers nearby are doing. For my 16.1 mu, I’ll keep most of the land in the usual wheat-maize rotation because that is the steadiest way to get grain and cash, and I’ll leave a smaller piece in cotton. I only have two people in the house, so I have to think about labor and timing, especially the few days between wheat harvest and maize sowing. The extension people talk about exact rates, but in practice I use round numbers and adjust by how the crop looks. This year I won’t cut fertilizer too hard, because if wheat or maize turns yellow from underfeeding, the yield loss hurts more than saving a little cash. But I also won’t push inputs too high, because pumping water and buying chemicals both cost money, and at my age I want a stable year more than gambling on a record yield.

For the wheat-maize land, I’ll put 12 mu into winter wheat and then summer maize right after harvest. On wheat I’ll use a local improved variety, sow in early October, put most of the phosphorus and part of the nitrogen at planting, then topdress once around jointing if the stand looks normal. With well water available, I plan three irrigations for wheat if the season is ordinary: one after sowing or before winter if soil is dry, one at jointing, and one around grain filling if needed. As soon as wheat comes off in June, I’ll direct-seed maize with minimal tillage so I don’t lose time or moisture. For cotton I’ll keep 4.1 mu. Cotton needs more watching and hand labor, so I won’t expand it. I’ll fertilize it a bit lighter than grain land, irrigate once or twice depending on rain, and spray only if insects or disease actually show up. That way I spread risk: grain gives me stability, cotton gives me some cash if the price is decent.
